[spoiler="Velho oeste de Bravanor"]
Há 2 séculos, por volta de 1808, Bravanor então sob o Imperador Dom João I, o primeiro imperador, e o primeiro ministro Duarte  Fonseca, o segundo com esse cargo que sucedeu Bonifácio em 1804, ao contrário de seu predecessor, Duarte era a favor da expansão contra terras indígenas e integração forçada dos locais, isso levou a aprovação da [b]Lei da Posse Livre[/b] em fevereiro de 1805,  lei essa que dizia:
[i]Art. 1º  Qualquer cidadão livre de origem nacional que deseje se fixar no interior do oeste será garantido um terreno livre de até 80 hectares.
Artigo 2º  A posse do terreno somente será validamente adquirida após o transcurso de três (3)anos, conforme o cumprimento das seguintes obrigações pelo possuidor:
I  Estabelecer residência permanente;
II  Cultivar a terra ou criar gado;
III  Não abandonar a propriedade por período superior a dois (2) anos consecutivos.
Artigo 3º  A propriedade será naturalmente transmitida a herdeiro direto, podendo ser concedida a terceiros apenas depois de reconhecida como posse produtiva.
Artigo 4º  Para a defesa contra possíveis hostilidades de nativos, os colonos serão providos de armamento e poderão organizar-se em forças de proteção, com a finalidade de resguardar a segurança de suas terras.
Artigo 5º  Caso a propriedade seja:
I  Abandonada por prazo superior a dois (2) anos;
II  Inapta à produção.
III  Desprovida de residência fixa pelo proprietário,
tal terreno poderá ser contestado por outros colonos, necessitando requerimento formal.
Artigo 6º  Considera-se produtiva a terra em que se verifique:
I  O cultivo de diversas espécies.
II  A criação extensiva de gado.

Artigo 7º  São especialmente recomendadas pelo governo as seguintes culturas:
I  Feijão;
II  Milho;
III  Arroz;
IV  Trigo.
V - Mandioca.

Artigo 8º  Ao colono que exceder a produção ordinária, ou que introduzir técnicas ou inovações, será concedida por este governo extensão adicional de terrenos, a título de prêmio por sua inovação e engenho.
[Etc etc]
[/i]
Embora a lei de facto tenha sido promulgada, a região ainda era habitada obviamente por diversos povos nativos, que incluíam:
[i]Kanupés, Kaingangs , Charruas[/i] (entre outros).
Esses povos que eram bem comuns na região entraram em conflitos constantes com os colonos locais, e como a lei permitia, eles eram muitas vezes caçados e mortos, já alguns colonos mais "leves" capturavam e "civilizavam" eles, isso é, forçavam eles  a abandonar suas tradições e cultura propria pelas nacionais, hoje por causa desse período conhecido como "[b]Pampas Selvagens[/b]", obviamente devido a geografia plana e de pradarias local e principalmente por ter sido um período sem lei, já que as terras novas eram pouco vigiadas de fato, quanto as populações indigenas:
[u]Charruas[/u]: tinham cerca de 50 mil antes, hoje tem acreditasse que apenas 60 pessoas Charruas , a maioria se miscigenou forçadamente.
[u]Kaingangs:[/u] eram 80 mil e se reduziram para  20 mil.
[u] Kanupés [/u]: eles já eram poucos, cerca de 10 mil, hoje foram totalmente extintos, eram vistos como selvagens e difíceis de "civilizar", mas na verdade só eram um povo que sempre foi resistente contra invasores.
Era comum que os colonos fossem para os pampas montados em seus cavalos e com laço para invadirem aldeias e capturaram mulheres de lá para se casarem com elas, as dando novos nomes.
O oeste ia muita além de só um lugar onde índios e colonos entravam em conflito , como uma nova terra relativamente grande, era de se esperar que rapidamente, sairia do controle das autoridades, esse período selvagem terminaria com a chegada da Imperatriz Isabel ao trono e a construção de novas ferrovias , abolição da  Lei da Posse Livre em 1890, e no geral maior controle dessa fronteira, até meados de 1900.
Esse período esteve em seu auge durante 3 vezes, a primeira entre 1810-1817, que terminou com a primeira Guerra do Contestado(causada pela insatisfação de colonos com a falta de definição de terras e propriedades, no fim o governo imperial concedeu muitas terras a coronéis esperando que fossem manter a lei na região, mas isso foi até 1820 com a Guerra dos Lenços Brancos, onde sob Damião de Figueiroa os antigos colonos se revoltaram com a promessa de receberem uma "terra santa", a guerra durou 7 anos e causou em 20 mil mortos, no fim os coronéis foram retirados de suas terras e  o império optou por deixar os colonos voltarem a terem suas terras, isso causou o segundo apogeu, que foi significativamente mais longo, de 1830 até 1865, um total de 35 anos,  entre roubos, conflitos com indígenas, a terra era vista como sem lei, mas rica em oportunidades.
Em 1865 até 1872 houve a Revolta dos Lenços Brancos , que foi uma revolta contra a construção de ferrovias na região que tiraram muitos colonos e deixaram eles sem chão, e muitas cidades acabaram abandonadas, essa guerra foi contra a empresa de acordo com os rebeldes não contra o império, onde jagunços, monges, cangaceiros e camponeses se uniram em uma guerra, lados bem opostos mas que se uniram contra o exército em mais de 100 mil rebeldes,  das 3 guerras do Contestado, essa foi sem dúvidas a mais brutal e terminou em 60 mil mortos de ambos os lados, a maioria porém, rebeldes, esse evento causou o declínio lento dos Pampas Selvagens até 1890.
*Glossario:
Cangaceiro:criminosos e bandidos.
Jagunço: cangaceiros  contratados como mercenários.
Coronel: não exatamente uma patente, nesse contexto grandes senhores de terra [i]eram coronéis.[/i]
[/spoiler]

[b] Kanupés e Olavo [/b]
Um compilado de histórias sobre a conquista de região.
O ano? 1808, 3 anos após a dita lei ser promulgada, Olavo Dias,  um colono alto e magro de uns 30 e poucos anos que havia já tido seus 80 hectares de terra aprovados, uma terra que ele usou para criar sua residência e cultivar mandioca e feijão, lá ele vivia com sua esposa uma mulher de origem Kanupé que ele nomeou Laura, e passou 1 ano a "civilizando", algo que ele se gabava.
Ele a deu um beijo de despedida e saiu a cavalo em direção a Encruzilhada, um pequeno assentamento que se localizava em uma estrada que se dividia em 3.
O lugar simplório, cujo centro era um botequim no armazém com uma bancada de madeira manchada e barris de bebida e bêbados caídos no chão.
"E foi assim que eu botei tudo aqueles índio pra correr!"
Olavo afirmou levantando um copo de cachaça no botequim do pequeno assentamento, os presentes se animaram com a história, até que outro, Gervásio Vieira, um homem robusto com barriga já meio a mostra, falou em um tom meio já afetado pela bebida:
"Hum...eu já ataquei sozinho uma aldeia e com um rifle fiz eles correrem de medo *[b]Burp[/b]* "ouvi dizer que me chamam de Heróña[1] claramente me chamam de herói!"
[1]=Heróña é um termo kanupé que significa "covarde"
Uma disputa então começou, cada um dos homens bêbados lá começou a contar histórias cada vez mais exageradas de vitórias contra indigenas, cada uma com coisas mais exageradas. Foi aí que , o homem mais são lá, o servidor das bebidas, conhecido como Jurandir Garrafeiro, que já era um nome conhecido na região por servir em vários botequins, finalmente falou ao ver as histórias já o incomodando, levantou a mão e bateu contra a bancada, o som reverberou por todo local e todos olharam para ele:
"Paguem suas contas e saiam desse bar, to afim de escutar mais história de borracho aqui não."
Olavo então, já com a cabeça desnorteada pela cachaça se apoiou na bancada e disse:
"Bah, mas nem mais um golezin de pinga não,  garrafeiro?"
Jurandir bufou enquanto limpava um dos copos com um pano velho:
"Paga tua conta Dias e volte antes que escureça e o bicho pegue pra ti ou sua querida 'Laura'."
Ele então pensou consigo próprio:
"Homens nojentos que se acham 'homens' apenas por isso...mas seus lugares já estão marcados no inferno...que clima pesado, até o ar parece sólido aqui..."
.
.
Enquanto a tensão continuava no bar, na simples cabana de madeira de Olavo, "Laura" era visitada por um homem esguio de pele morena, e cabelo escuro negro que ia até seus ombros com algumas mechas coladas em sua testa, como se ele estivesse suando pela corrida, sua pele marcada por algumas cicatrizes simples e pinturas corporais ocre e coberta por uma simples tanga de couro e um colar de sementes, ele estendeu a mão para a janela da cabana, onde "Laura" estava, ele então olhou para ela diretamente em seus olhos castanhos que pareciam com medo, mas não do homem, de outra coisa.
"Tayrikua..."
Ele disse com a voz ofegante, aquele era o verdadeiro nome de "Laura", o homem ela conhecia, era seu irmão mais novo, o qual tinha só 17 anos ela pôs a mão na janela contra a dele e falou:
"Ñanguarú..."
Ela então abriu a janela, e saiu para o lado de seu irmão, o avental de linho se agarrou em um prego e rasgou um pouco, mas ela não se importou, só queria fugir daquele lugar que ficou presa por um ano, eles se abraçaram, o corpo calejado de seu irmão contra a roupa de linho dela se contrastavam, um gesto de afeto,  Ñanguarú então passou a mão no rosto da irmã, ele murmurou para si:
"O que eles fizeram com você irmã..."
Mas então rapidamente olhou para os lados para verificar se nenhum dos homens pálidos estava, e então disse:
"Vamos embora daqui antes que eles cheguem ok?"
Ela então assentiu, e agarrou a mão do irmão e ambos fugiram para as pradarias em direção a onde quer que ele estivesse indo.
Ñanguarú a guiava agarrando com força, enquanto olhava para os arredores, cada tropeço era uma respiração prendida, até que chegaram próximos de um pequeno morro para descansarem brevemente, era seguro, aquela hora no entardecer os colonos estavam bêbados demais para irem a "caçada", Tayrikua suspirou e disse:
"Vamos para onde, irmão?"
Ele então sorriu meio cansado, os dentes brancos pareciam brilhantes, ele então a respondeu:
"Para um lugar seguro irmã...para um lugar melhor..."
Após alguns minutos de descanso, eles voltaram a andarem pelas pradarias e o capinzal até encontrarem outra elevação...
No topo do morro era onde estava o novo lar. A aldeia era um local construído em um morro cercado por estacas de madeira pontiagudas, as ocas eram baixas mas longas pois as famílias kanupés são notavelmente extensas, no centro da aldeia uma grande fogueira de erguia e um mapa ao lado, que era feito com várias folhas entrelaçadas com pigmentos vermelhos para perigo, azul para água, e preto para trilhas, um dos anciões da aldeia, um velho que usava um manto plumado chegou perto da moça e a analisou brevemente, e então sorriu e disse pondo a mão em seu ombro:
"Bem vinda de volta,  Tayrikua.".
[b] História de Celestino-1808.[/b]
Longe de Encruzilhada, e da tensão de Olavo, mais ao sul vivia Celestino Gonçalves, que conseguirá fazer suas terras produtivas com a criação de gado e cultivo de feijão e milho, sua cabana era mais simples e pequena, onde vivia com sua esposa, uma mulher de pele morena como ele que veio junto dele de São José, alguns chamavam ele de um homem frouxo demais por ele tratar sua esposa bem, ao contrário de muitos, enquanto estava fora buscando por gado para sua fazenda, ele deitou-se sobre seu cavalo crioulo o qual repousava no capinzal, tomou um tempo para olhar para os céus, e então escutou um tumulto vindo de um mato mais alto a sua direita, lá ele viu vultos nus, kaingangs, e então agarrou seu rifle, não era para atirar, mas para de defender,  3 jovens Kaingangs, que andavam desnudos, o encararam, não estavam armados, nem nada, mas a tensão ainda era inegável, o bravanês sentiu seu coração bater forte contra seu peito em preocupação, mas, ao contrário do que ele esperava, os índios pareciam querer oferecer algo, quando ele se aproximou com cautela, eles deixaram um presente e então fugiram.
Celestino se aproximou do presente, parecia um pedaço de carne defumada de cervo sobre um prato de madeira enrolada por uma folha de araucária que dizia em letras rabiscadas pouco legíveis "paz".
Surpreso pelo presente, Celestino o pegou com gratidão, e então deu um leve chute em seu equino, apenas para o fazer levantar,  dizendo:
"Levanta Pé de Pano"
O cavalo obedeceu, e então Celestino subiu se preparando para voltar para sua cabana, onde sua esposa, Maria aguardava.
As mãos dela calejadas pelo serviço, e expressão serena e calma a destacavam de outras mulheres que já pareciam bem menos aparentes para a suas idades, Maria era bem cuidada em sua aparência no geral, surpresa pela carne já feita, ela perguntou para seu marido:
"De onde trouxe essa carne... Tino?"
Era como ela chamava seu marido, embora já soubesse a reposta, ela resolveu perguntar mesmo assim, ele a respondeu:
"De vizinhos que decidiram me ajudar na minha caçada Mari, olha só isso."
Ela deu um sorriso sutil, já sabendo quem eram os "vizinhos" que ele dizia, no dia seguinte, Maria a pedido de Celestino foi deixar uma oferenda para os índios que ajudaram ele, uma enxada velha que eles já não usavam mais e estava servindo apenas para tomar espaço, quando o sol começou a se por, a enxada já não estava mais lá e marcas de pés descalços levavam para um capinzal.
O artigo 4 previa que os colonos poderiam atirar contra os "selvagens" a vontade, mas, nem todos seguiriam a risca, homens como Celestino são um exemplo perfeito, uma harmonia a qual tolos como Olavo jamais entenderiam...
[b] Historia de Benício Moreira-1809. [/B]
O justiceiro dos Pampas, um homem que fazia a lei por si, Benício Moreira viveu entre 1769 até sua morte na Revolta dos Lenços Brancos  1824.
O justiceiro dos Pampas era um homem de corpo robusto e pouco cabelo, usava um chapéu estilo um sombreiro de palha e um lenço branco no pescoço, em seu cinto além de um rifle usava uma peixeira(faça) e botas de tropeiro, um colete de couro e por fim duas cartucheiras cruzadas em seu peito, ele fumou um charuto grosso e então o jogou no chão, ele pegou um cartaz de procurado :
[b] ULISSES RABO DE CAVALO[/b]
PROCURADO VIVO OU MORTO.
RECOMPENSA: 15 mil Réis.
"Quinze mil Réis pra esse guri aí?"
Benício franziu a testa em dúvida se o homem no cartaz realmente valia tudo isso, era rapaz de pelo menos uns 20 anos, o desenho dele no cartaz tinha um nariz largo e olhos escuros e um cabelo estilo rabo de cavalo que era bem grande e ia até suas costas.
Ele olhou para trás do cartaz para analisar o motivo de sua recompensa acima da média (5 mil  Réis para a região) , lá dizia:
"Hm...roubou cavalos e gado, mantimentos, e contrabando de charque e pinga...modesto, parece um pouco exagerado até..."
Ele comentou arrumando o papel amassado em seu bolso.
"20 anos e pouco e esse piá já tem uma recompensa bem modesta hein..."
Ele lançou um sorriso e lambeu os próprios lábios:
"Irei caçar qualquer cangaceiro até o inferno como eu mesmo já prometi contra qualquer um desses trastes..."
O justiceiro então partiu de lá e foi seguindo rastros e rastros, até chegar em Encruzilhada, ele sabia que o "Garrafeiro" poderia ser também um excelente informante já que o mesmo já lidou com diversos outros botequins. A aura que o justiceiros carregava era forte e emanava , os outros beberrões se afastaram quando Benício bateu o cartaz contra a bancada, O Garrafeiro olhou e disse:
"Sempre direto ao ponto Benício...bom dia."
O justiceiro cumprimentou de volta com um gesto, e então apontou para o cartaz:
"Jurandir...você é os olhos e ouvidos desse pampas, certamente deve saber desse jovem cangaceiro."
Jurandir hesitou por um momento, limpou o copo em sua mão por alguns instantes antes de finalmente responder:
"Veja...Ulisses, um guri metido a besta que apanhou mais que o pai, e agora fica na Estância de Esteira achando que o mundo deve algo a ele...mas veja, eu vendo cachaça e bebida pra borracho, não informações pra..."
Benício sorriu, já tinha oque queria, retirou um pouco de dinheiro, cerca de mil Réis e colocou no balcão e saiu, os olhos de Jurandir brilharam com o dinheiro, ele então sussurrou;
"...mas por um preço...eu aceito, Benício!"
Ele gritou para o justiceiro, que parou para escutar:
"Só saiba que ele não está sozinho, o Rabo de Cavalo criou a própria gangue, os Rabo de Cavalo, dizem ser uns nove..."
Moraes apenas sorriu rolando a peixeira entre os dedos, disse:
"9 cabeças...mais o próprio líder, 10..."
Ele então saiu do botequim subindo no cavalo negro dele,  partiu para os pampas em direção do último lugar onde Ulisses estava. Ele não precisava forçar, o animal galopou rapidamente conforme o guia de Benício, até que finalmente notou uma fumaça, poderia ser qualquer coisa, um acampamento, aldeia, mas não era uma região de morro ou de Rio, nem com muitos animais, parecia querer continuar isolada, foi isso que Benício foi verificar, ao deixar seu cavalo ele se recostou em uma rocha e observou, 9 homens, e mais um dentro de uma tenda, aquele era o refúgio da gangue dos Rabo de Cavalo, seus membros erguiam uma bandeira com um cavalo relinchando e com as patas levantadas, seus membros eram notáveis por terem rabos de cavalo, obviamente, e o maior era o de Ulisses, fácil de reconhecer.
Assim Benício partiu a observar, não iria os atacar diretamente, ele não era um herói de histórias é claro, então aguardou com paciência até o auge da tarde, onde um jovem de olhar nervoso foi designado para a vigília, o justiceiro aproveitou a oportunidade e sorrateiro se aproximou por trás e colocou a peixeira contra a garganta do garoto e disse:
"Não pretendo o matar tampinha, me diz onde tá teu chefe ."
Nervoso e com medo, o vigia apontou para uma das tendas,o justiceiro então o nocauteou com um golpe na nuca e então pegou uma pedra, e a jogou para outro lado chamando atenção dos membros da gangue.
O justiceiro partiu para a tenda que o garoto apontou, onde encontrou Ulisses ajustando um revólver, ao ouvir o invasor ele se virou para atirar, mas Benício foi mais rápido, lançou sua peixeira que perfurou sua mão e o forçou a largar o revólver, o Rabo de Cavalo gritou, avisando o restante da gangue, Benício bufou:
"Desgraça..."
O justiceiro arrancou a lâmina da mão do Rabo de Cavalo e então saiu em direção da fogueira, com sua bota de campeiro chutou espalhando a brasa para uma das tendas que tinha pólvora, explodindo alguns dos homens, os poucos lá entraram em desespero para salvarem os mantimentos do acampamento, aproveitando o caos, o justiceiro amarrou e colocou Ulisses em seu ombro e saiu correndo até seu cavalo, e zombou:
"Parece que seus homens estão mais preocupados com o próprio tesouro que você.*
[b]TCHOOSSS[/b].
O som de um disparo de rifle ecoou, a arma engatilhada foi disparada contra Benício, que por uma fração de segundo  congelou, e então desviou, o tiro passando de raspão em seu rosto, ele se virou pegando um revólver e atirando contra o atirador, não sabendo se acertou ou não, e então voltou a correr, enquanto escutava os devaneios do rabo de cavalo.
"Hein quer dinheiro? Eu posso lhe dar o que você quiser só me desamarre!"
"A CALA BOCA."
ele rugiu batendo o revólver contra o cangaceiro o deixando inconsciente, então montou no cavalo e partiu para Encruzilhada, onde esperava ganhar uns 15 mil Réis, e comprar alguns charutos e armas novas, e foi assim que ele partindo para o horizonte derrubou o "Rabo de Cavalo".
[b] São Damião de Figueiroa .[/b]
Era assim que os seguidores de Damião de Figueiroa o chamavam, ele foi quem se revoltou contra os coronéis e liderou a Revolta dos Lenços Brancos, ele nada mais era que um pastor de uma pequena capela, mas com um carisma inegável,  e quem criou os primeiros jagunços, os ex cangaceiros contratados como mercenários... 
Damião não era um herói, nem nada nasceu em um rancho pobre e era um simples pastor de uma pequena capela em Boa Vista, não carregava a mesma bíblia que os altares de São José, apenas um livro de salmos e versículos com sua própria interpretação deles.
Ele era de estatura média, sem traços muito interessantes, apenas um pastor como outros, em 1817 porém, com o fim da Primeira Guerra do Contestado, e a vinda dos Coronéis com documentos de São José aprovados pelo imperador,  e a falta de limitações fez os coronéis essencialmente tomarem terras de outros colonos menores que passaram os últimos 10 anos lutando contra os indigenas e conquistando a região, sua capela logo deixará de ser um mero centro de consolo, mas um lar para os desabrigados, a cidade deixaria de ser Boa Vista, o povo a chamaria de "Esperança".
Naquela humilde capela encontraram consolo, e voz, O pastor não pregava violência, mas exigia justiça divina. De acordo. Ok ele os coronéis não eram opressão, mas um teste divino e como tal a ser superado.
No início os coronéis não se importaram afinal , para eles não passava de um simples pastor pregando , o movimento passou a ganhar poder, e um nome, [b]Os Lenços Brancos[/b], devido ao movimento usar lenços brancos para os diferenciar, foi fundado.
"...derrubem os coronéis, e assim a terra santa será conquistada".
Isso é oque ele dizia, de acordo com ele, a terra santa era o próprio oeste,que foi conquistada e agora deve ser reconquistada.
A revolta começou em 1820, após uma procissão pacífica durante os pampas, um dos coronéis abriu fogo contra os fiéis, e issose ergueu em protesto contra a opressão, muitos responderam, camponeses miseráveis, tropeiros a até cangaceiros absolvidos que foram chamados Jagunços, mesmo lendas como o então aposentado Justiceiro dos Pampas , Benício Moraes respondeu se juntando a revolta ,o exército santo, como eles mesmos se chamavam, se moveu.
Eles se moviam como guerrilheiros ágeis, as terras dos Coronéis eram invadidas, e eles eram mortos, suas famílias expelidas, e as terras eram devolvidas aos seus antigos donos, os jagunços eram mais brutais no entanto, invadiam as casas-grandes e executavam o coronel e sua família como um todo, o profeta São Damião muitas vezes era visto usando seu lenço branco em seu pescoço, uma manta colorida desbotada, enquanto usava vestes simples por baixo e com botas de tropeiro, sempre usando um cajado velho de madeira, e com adornos de rosários e colares com sementes de arroz.
Sua aparência não era nada diferente da de um homem comum, pele marcada pelo sol, e com cara de uns 40 anos , mas sempre caminhava com confiança e calma absoluta, ele andava pelos campos enquanto curava feridos de uma forma descrita como [b]mágica[/b] , como se a própria pele dos feridos de curasse com sua mera presença.
Um caso excepcional de seus milagres foi salvar um garoto chamado Teodoro que havia sofrido um destrutivo corte de facão que quase o matou, no entanto Damião pareceu tecer sua pele com um gesto, e então a curou, como se nunca tivesse existido sequer um ferimento.
[b] organização dos lenços brancos.[/b]
O Messias era o líder, Damião Figueiroa, ou São Damião.

Em 1865 até 1872 houve a Revolta dos Lenços Brancos , que foi uma revolta contra a construção de ferrovias na região que tiraram muitos colonos e deixaram eles sem chão, e muitas cidades acabaram abandonadas, essa guerra foi contra a empresa de acordo com os rebeldes não contra o império, onde jagunços, monges, cangaceiros e camponeses se uniram em uma guerra, lados bem opostos mas que se uniram contra o exército em mais de 100 mil rebeldes,  das 3 guerras do Contestado, essa foi sem dúvidas a mais brutal e terminou em 60 mil mortos de ambos os lados, a maioria porém, rebeldes, esse evento causou o declínio lento dos Pampas Selvagens até 1890.

[b] Kanupés and Olavo [/b] A compilation of stories about the conquest of the region. The year? 1808, 3 years after the said law was enacted, Olavo Dias, a tall and thin settler in his early 30s who had already had his 80 hectares of land approved, land he used to build his residence and cultivate cassava and beans, lived there with his wife, a woman of Kanupé origin whom he named Laura, and spent a year "civilizing" her, something he boasted about. He gave her a farewell kiss and left on horseback toward Encruzilhada, a small settlement located at a three-way crossroads.

The simple place, whose center was a tavern in the warehouse with a stained wooden counter and barrels of liquor and drunkards collapsed on the floor.
"And thats how I drove all those Indians away!" Olavo declared, raising a glass of cachaça in the tavern of the small settlement, the crowd cheered at the story, until another, Gervásio Vieira, a robust man with his belly half exposed, spoke in a tone already somewhat affected by drink:
"Hum... I once attacked a village alone and with a rifle made them run in fear [b]Burp[/b] I heard they call me Heróña[1] clearly they call me a hero!"
[1]=Heróña is a Kanupé term meaning "coward"

A dispute then began, each of the drunken men there started telling increasingly exaggerated stories of victories against natives, each one more far-fetched than the last.

Thats when the most sober man there, the drink server known as Jurandir Garrafeiro, who was already a known name in the region for serving in several taverns, finally spoke as the stories began to annoy him. He raised his hand and slammed it against the counter, the sound echoing throughout the place and everyone turned to look at him:
"Pay your tabs and get out of this bar, Im not in the mood to hear another drunkards tale."

Olavo then, already dizzy from the cachaça, leaned against the counter and said:
"Bah, not even one more sip of pinga, Garrafeiro?"

Jurandir snorted while cleaning one of the cups with an old rag:
"Pay your tab, Dias, and head back before night falls and trouble comes for you or your dear 'Laura'."

He then thought to himself:
"Disgusting men who think theyre 'men' only because of this but their places are already marked in hell the air here is so heavy it feels solid..."

. .

While the tension lingered in the bar, in Olavos simple wooden hut, "Laura" was visited by a slender, dark-skinned man with black hair down to his shoulders with a few strands stuck to his forehead as if he had been sweating from running, his skin marked by simple scars and ochre body paint and covered only by a simple leather loincloth and a necklace of seeds.

He stretched his hand toward the huts window, where "Laura" was. He then looked directly into her brown eyes, which seemed fearfulbut not of the man, of something else.

"Tayrikua..." He said, his voice breathless. That was "Lauras" true name. The man she knew, he was her younger brother, only 17 years old. She placed her hand on the window against his and spoke:
"Ñanguarú..."

She then opened the window and stepped out beside her brother, her linen apron snagging on a nail and tearing a bit, but she didnt care, she only wanted to flee that place she had been trapped for a year. They embraced, her brothers calloused body contrasting with her linen clothing, a gesture of affection. Ñanguarú then brushed his hand against his sisters face and murmured to himself:
"What did they do to you, sister..."

But then quickly looked around to check if any of the pale men were nearby, and then said:
"Lets leave here before they arrive, ok?"

She nodded, grabbing her brothers hand, and both fled into the prairies, heading wherever he was going. Ñanguarú guided her, holding tightly while scanning the surroundings. Each stumble was a held breath, until they reached a small hill to rest briefly. It was safefor at that hour in the late afternoon, the settlers were too drunk to go "hunting."

Tayrikua sighed and said:
"Where are we going, brother?"

He smiled, somewhat tired, his white teeth shining, and replied:
"To a safe place, sister to a better place..."

After a few minutes of rest, they resumed walking through the prairies and tall grass until they reached another rise...

At the top of the hill was their new home. The village was built on a hill surrounded by pointed wooden stakes, the longhouses were low but long, since Kanupé families were notably large. In the center of the village, a great fire burned and a map lay beside it, made of woven leaves with red pigments for danger, blue for water, and black for trails. One of the village elders, an old man wearing a feathered cloak, approached the young woman, looked her over briefly, then smiled and placed a hand on her shoulder:
"Welcome back, Tayrikua."

[b] Story of Celestino - 1808. [/b]

Far from Encruzilhada and Olavos tension, further south lived Celestino Gonçalves, who had managed to make his lands productive with cattle raising and the cultivation of beans and corn. His cabin was simpler and smaller, where he lived with his wife, a dark-skinned woman like him who had come with him from São José. Some called him too soft a man because he treated his wife well, unlike many others.

While out searching for cattle for his farm, he lay upon his Criollo horse resting in the tall grass, taking a moment to look at the sky, when he heard a commotion coming from taller brush to his right. There he saw naked silhouettesKaingangsand grabbed his rifle. Not to shoot, but to defend.

Three young Kaingangs, walking unclothed, stared at him. They were unarmed, but the tension was undeniable. The Bravanese settler felt his heart pounding against his chest in worry. But, unlike what he expected, the natives seemed to want to offer something. When he approached cautiously, they left a gift and then fled.

Celestino approached the giftit seemed to be a piece of smoked venison on a wooden plate wrapped in an araucaria leaf, which bore in barely legible scribbled letters the word "peace."

Surprised by the gift, Celestino picked it up gratefully, then gave a light nudge to his horse, just to make it rise, saying:
"Get up, Pé de Pano."

The horse obeyed, and Celestino mounted, preparing to return to his cabin, where his wife Maria awaited him.

Her hands were calloused from work, yet her serene and calm expression set her apart from other women who already seemed much older than their years. Maria was well cared for in her appearance overall. Surprised by the ready-made meat, she asked her husband:
"Where did you get this meat Tino?"

Thats what she called her husband, although she already knew the answer, she asked anyway. He replied:
"From neighbors who decided to help me with my hunt, Mari, just look at this."

She gave a subtle smile, already knowing who the "neighbors" he spoke of were.

The next day, at Celestinos request, Maria left an offering for the natives who had helped himan old hoe they no longer used and which was only taking up space. By sunset, the hoe was gone, and barefoot tracks led into the tall grass.

Article 4 stated that settlers could shoot the "savages" at will, but not all followed it strictly. Men like Celestino are a perfect example, a harmony that fools like Olavo could never understand...
[b] Story of Benício Moreira - 1809 [/b]

The avenger of the Pampas, a man who enforced the law by himself, Benício Moreira lived from 1769 until his death in the Revolt of the White Handkerchiefs in 1824.

The avenger of the Pampas was a man with a robust body and little hair, wore a straw-style sombrero and a white scarf around his neck. On his belt, in addition to a rifle, he carried a machete and muleteer boots, a leather vest, and finally two bandoliers crossed over his chest. He smoked a thick cigar and then threw it to the ground. He picked up a wanted poster:

[b] ULISSES HORSETAIL [/b]
WANTED DEAD OR ALIVE.
REWARD: 15 thousand Réis.

"Fifteen thousand Réis for this kid?"

Benício frowned, doubtful if the man on the poster was really worth that much. He was a boy of at least 20 years old; the drawing on the poster showed him with a broad nose, dark eyes, and a large ponytail that reached his back.

He looked at the back of the poster to analyze the reason for the above-average reward (5 thousand Réis for the region). It read:
"Hm stole horses and cattle, provisions, and smuggled dried meat and cachaça modest, seems a bit exaggerated even..."

He commented, straightening the crumpled paper in his pocket.
"Just over 20 and this kid already has a decent reward, huh"

He gave a smile and licked his lips:
"I will hunt any cangaceiro to hell as I have promised myself against any of these scoundrels"

The avenger then left and followed track after track until reaching Encruzilhada. He knew that "Garrafeiro" could also be an excellent informant, since he had dealt with various other taverns. The aura the avenger carried was strong and emanated; the other drinkers stepped back when Benício slammed the poster against the counter. Garrafeiro looked and said:
"Always straight to the point, Benício good morning."

The avenger greeted back with a gesture and then pointed to the poster:
"Jurandir you are the eyes and ears of these pampas, you must certainly know about this young cangaceiro."

Jurandir hesitated for a moment, wiped the glass in his hand for a few moments before finally responding:
"Look Ulisses, a cocky kid whos been beaten more than his father, now staying at the Esteira Ranch thinking the world owes him but look, I sell cachaça and drinks to drunks, not information to"

Benício smiled, already having what he wanted, took out some money, about a thousand Réis, placed it on the counter, and left. Jurandirs eyes gleamed at the money; he then whispered:
"but for a price I accept, Benício!"

He shouted to the avenger, who stopped to listen:
"Just know hes not alone, Horse Tail created his own gang, the Horse Tails, said to be about nine"

Moraes just smiled, rolling the machete between his fingers, and said:
"9 heads plus the leader himself, 10"

He then left the tavern, mounting his black horse, heading into the Pampas toward the last place Ulisses was seen. He didnt need to push, the animal galloped quickly under Benícios guidance, until he finally noticed smoke. It could be anything: a camp, a village, but it wasnt a hilly or river region, nor with many animalsit seemed intentionally isolated. Thats what Benício went to check. Leaving his horse, he leaned against a rock and observed: 9 men, and one more inside a tent. That was the refuge of the Horse Tail gang, its members raising a flag with a rearing horse, their members notable for having ponytails, obviously, and the largest was Ulisses, easy to recognize.

Benício began to observe. He wouldnt attack directlyhe wasnt a hero from stories, of courseso he waited patiently until late afternoon, when a nervous-looking youth was assigned to the watch. The avenger seized the opportunity and stealthily approached from behind, placing the machete against the boys throat and said:
"I dont intend to kill you, kid, tell me where your boss is."

Nervous and scared, the watchman pointed to one of the tents. The avenger then knocked him out with a strike to the neck, picked up a stone, and threw it elsewhere to draw the gang members attention.

The avenger went toward the tent the boy had indicated, where he found Ulisses adjusting a revolver. Hearing the intruder, he turned to shoot, but Benício was faster, throwing his machete that pierced his hand and forced him to drop the revolver. Horse Tail shouted, alerting the rest of the gang. Benício snorted:
"Damn"

The avenger ripped the blade from Horse Tails hand and then went toward the campfire. With his boots, he kicked embers into one of the tents that had gunpowder, exploding some of the men. The few inside panicked trying to save the camps provisions. Taking advantage of the chaos, the avenger tied up and slung Ulisses over his shoulder and ran to his horse, mocking:
"Seems your men care more about their own treasure than you."

[b]TCHOOSSS[/b].

The sound of a rifle shot echoed; the cocked weapon fired at Benício. For a fraction of a second, he froze, then dodged, the bullet grazing his face. He turned, grabbed a revolver, and fired at the shooter, not knowing if he hit, then ran again, listening to Horse Tails ramblings:
"Hein, want money? I can give you whatever you want, just untie me!"
"SHUT UP."

He roared, striking the cangaceiros with the revolver, rendering him unconscious, then mounted his horse and headed to Encruzilhada, hoping to earn about 15 thousand Réis and buy some cigars and new weapons. And thats how, riding into the horizon, he took down the "Horse Tail."
[b] São Damião de Figueiroa [/b]

Thats what Damião de Figueiroas followers called him. He was the one who rebelled against the coronels and led the Revolt of the White Handkerchiefs. He was nothing more than a pastor of a small chapel, but with undeniable charisma, and he created the first jagunços, the ex-cangaceiros hired as mercenaries

Damião was not a hero, nor anything special. He was born in a poor ranch and was a simple pastor of a small chapel in Boa Vista, carrying not the same Bible as the altars of São José, only a book of psalms and verses with his own interpretation of them.

He was of average height, without striking features, just a pastor like any other. However, in 1817, with the end of the First Contestado War, the arrival of the coronels with documents from São José approved by the emperor, and the lack of limitations, the coronels essentially took lands from smaller colonists who had spent the last 10 years fighting against the indigenous and conquering the region. His chapel soon ceased to be a mere center of solace, becoming a home for the homeless. The city ceased to be Boa Vista; the people would call it Hope.

In that humble chapel, they found comfort and a voice. The pastor did not preach violence but demanded divine justice. According to him, the coronels were not oppression, but a divine test, and as such, to be overcome.

At first, the coronels did not care. After all, to them he was just a simple pastor preaching. But the movement began to gain power and a name: [b]The White Handkerchiefs[/b], because the movement used white handkerchiefs to differentiate themselves. It was founded.

"bring down the coronels, and the holy land will be conquered."

Thats what he said. According to him, the holy land was the west itself, which had been conquered and now must be reconquered.

The revolt began in 1820. After a peaceful procession across the pampas, one of the coronels opened fire on the faithful, and that sparked a protest against oppression. Many responded: miserable peasants, muleteers, and even absolved cangaceiros called Jagunços. Even legends like the then-retired Justiceiro dos Pampas, Benício Moraes, joined the revolt. The holy army, as they called themselves, moved.

They moved like agile guerrillas. The coronels lands were invaded, they were killed, their families expelled, and the lands returned to their former owners. The jagunços were even more brutal, invading the big houses and executing the coronel and his family as a whole. The prophet São Damião was often seen wearing his white handkerchief around his neck, a faded colorful blanket, while wearing simple clothes underneath and muleteer boots, always carrying an old wooden staff adorned with rosaries and rice seed necklaces.

His appearance was nothing different from an ordinary man, sun-weathered skin, looking about 40 years old, but he always walked with confidence and absolute calm. He wandered the fields while healing the wounded in a way described as [b]magical[/b], as if the very skin of the injured healed in his mere presence.

An exceptional case of his miracles was saving a boy named Teodoro, who had suffered a destructive machete cut that almost killed him. Damião seemed to weave his skin with a gesture and then healed him, as if the wound had never existed.

[b] Organization of the White Handkerchiefs [/b]

The Messiah was the leader, Damião Figueiroa, or São Damião.

Below him were the 4 Sacred Knights:
[b]Master of Arms[/b] Benício Moraes.
[b]Master of Horses[/b] Bento Serrano.
[b]Master of Altars[/b] Celestino Gonçalves.
[b]Guardian of Faith[/b] Lourenço Costa.

Below them were the Devoted Blades, all women. They had no special titles, called South Wind, North Wind, East Wind, and West Wind.

[b]South Wind:[/b] Maria Gonçalves (Celestinos space)
[b]North Wind:[/b] Josefina dos Santos
[b]West Wind:[/b] Gertrudes Costa
[b]East Wind:[/b] Francisca Vieira

[b]Eyes of the Pampas[/b] was the title given to Jurandir Garrafeiro, an informant serving both sides, only taking what paid more.

The army was composed of a mix of militiamenmen, women, and elderscalled Divine Lancers. The tropeiros were the ones on horseback, making up most of the force and moving quickly.
[b]Esperança, 1824.[/b]

The Messiah picked up a guitar, his followers gathered around a bonfire, and he began to play along with a harmonica by his side.

"Your pilcha marked by bullets,
proved loyalty
You freed the frets in the rusgent wind,
drawing the dagger with cries of freedom"

The crowd sang along with the song, full of excitement and energy, while the fire crackled under the moonlight. Benício, the Justiceiro dos Pampas, sharpened his peixeira while leaning against a rock, observing Damião. He was not blindly faithful like many of the believers, he simply saw him as true justice. On the other side, Celestino and Maria were also presentnot mere colonists anymore, now high-ranking officers in the army of the Faithful.

After the music ended, Damião stood tall with his staff and began a speech.

"Brothers and sisters!"

He raised his voice:

"The cowardly coronel Valente will be our target tomorrow morning. As soon as the sun rises, we will advance to the Chapadão farm and destroy one of the dens of this evil that corrodes the holy land!"

The faithful rose in response, white-handkerchief flags waving, clearly exciteda fervor whose heat rivaled that of the bonfire.

The march began at dawn. Muleteers armed with sickles and spears, infantry with rifles, all ready for the invasion. Right behind were the Justiceiro dos Pampas and Master of Horses Bento Serrano. Years of war had turned the farm from a rural property into what Damião called a fortress: tall palisades dominated, and wire nets above prevented entry. Thats when the justiceiro suggested:

"Bento, I need you to launch a charge at the main gate. Ill find a way to open a path through the west."

Serrano hesitated at firstit was risky, he knew, and Benício was no longer youngbut there was no choice but to trust the plan.

Hidden, small but wide enough for a man to pass, the entry point was a fetid darkness Benício had to traverse. But justice would prevail. Emerging through one of the pig pens, he nearly vomited but resisted, listening to the warriors noise at the gate. Shots rang out as he dashed, firing his rifle from behind the farm guards, then slashing with his knife, tearing through flesh. Confusion spread among the guards.

The gate was opened, and chaos erupted. Thats when the justiceiro saw [i]him.[/i]

Valente was a large, robust man, aiming his rifle not at the chaos but at Bento, who led one of the charges.

"NO!"

Benício shouted, throwing himself against his comrade. The shot echoed across the battlefield, grazing his belt, ripping leather, burning his vest and shirt. He fell to the ground. The Master of Horses looked concerned, but Benício laughed:

"Youll have to try harder than that to take me down."

He stood, feeling tension in his shoulders, moving away from his ally, boots sinking in the muddy ground toward Valente on the veranda, then entered the main house. Valente aimed at him and smiled, firing again, but Benício ran, breaking through the door. The shot only shattered the window. Valente lunged at him, causing the justiceiro to drop his peixeira. Benício overpowered him, grabbing him with wide hands and throwing him against a wooden table, breaking it. Valente stamped on Benício with a sinister grin:

"Die, you filthy dog!"

Desperate, Benício groped for something to defend himself, the air thinning, pressure building on his neck. He grabbed a splintered piece of the broken table and drove it into Valente, forcing him to release his grip. Benício took a moment to breathe, struggling to rise, heart hammering. Valente, limping, advanced again, grabbing Benícios neck, but he used the mans weak leg to his advantage, kicking hard, weakening the hold. He spun his body, making the large man crash through the window. Benício seized the moment, lunging with his peixeira, stabbing the robust man.

In a disgusting babble of curses and blood, Valente struck once more, using a slaughter knife that cut Benícios side, leaving a dark red mark. He staggered, and after killing the coronel, reached the gate where victory was already celebrated. A white-handkerchief flag was raised atop the farm. He fell to his knees; the celebration turned from hostility to despair. One of the horsemen was fatally wounded, and the only one who could save him was Damião. The Messiah bent toward Benício, ready to act, but he gripped Damiãos arm:

"Ndont save me, dont hold me, Damião Ive done my part now let justice do the rest"

The voice gurgled through blood. He looked at the faithful warriors, smiled, and finally closed his eyes for eternal rest. His black horse neighed softly, then lay down beside his fallen friend.

[b]Serro dos Anjos, 1827.[/b]

Seven years of war, tens of thousands of deaths, but an effect that reverberated across the nation. Since the imperial army moved in, the revolt had become a series of guerrilla operations, now reduced to no more than 1,000 militiamen. Most of the Devoted Blades and all Knights were exterminated, leaving only Maria and Francisca. Damião climbed a high rock, using it as an altar, and declared:

"Brothers and sisters."

As he spoke and raised his staff, a mist enveloped them, obscuring the vision of the imperials. The Baron of Caçapava cursed:

"Damn it seems even the heavens want to protect this madman! ADVANCE TO THE HILL!"

He ordered, pointing his saber at the rebels.

"The empire does not know that faith cannot be killed, but spreads. They think they have cornered us, surrounded us, but they are [b]wrong[/b]."

He pointed his staff at everyone in front of him.

"Each one here is already victorious, each one already a guardian of these pampas. For hope, FOR THE HOLY LAND, DEFEND THIS SACRED HILL!"

The sound of advancing soldiers began. Soldiers with bayonets fired mercilessly as rebels were massacred, blood staining their white handkerchiefs. Francisca asked:

"Holiness, what do we do now?"

Damião smiled:

"Focus on the now, my dear sister."

He stepped in front of her, staff taking shots behind him yet remaining unscathed. He declared:

"Aarons Staff is unbreakable. Surrender and accept the divine light!"

He raised the staff again, reflecting the sun into a blinding beam, stunning the imperials and giving a brief advantage. But the imperials were poised to win. One by one, they fell

Maria fell among the bodies to avoid death. Francisca took a fatal shot to the heart. Only Damião remained standing. The Baron of Caçapava, curious, finally approached the rebel leader:

"Surrender, madman. Your madness has ruled these pampas far longer than it should"

Damião raised his arms, stepping backnot in fear, but as if declaiming:

"Who is victorious here? I fought for Gods will and an altar, you for a distant emperor and a hill. I for the people and the end of the coronels who among us truly wins?"

He spoke calmly, a terrifying peace in his tone. Then, in a surprising gesture, he raised his staff and said:

"The Holy Land is not conquered with blood, but sanctified with it!"

With surprising force, the White Handkerchief pierces the staff into the ground, even breaking the altar he stood on, then fell. A thunderous sound and tremor toppled many soldiers. Those who remained forced themselves to kneel. The Baron, shocked, exclaimed:

"Earthquake? Even the earth sides with this madman?!"

As he fell, Damiãos Bible dropped with him. One verse was marked inside:
[i]"He whose voice [b]then shook the Earth[/b]."[/i]

Maria, having seen everything, gripped the white handkerchief around her neck, also shocked, murmuring:

"So thats what the prophet meant?"

On the other side, horses neighed and soldiers kneeled as dust rose, sabers embedded in the ground, rifles fallen before them

The simple place, whose center was a tavern in the warehouse with a stained wooden counter and barrels of liquor and drunkards collapsed on the floor.

A dispute then began, each of the drunken men there started telling increasingly exaggerated stories of victories against natives, each one more far-fetched than the last.

"Pay your tabs and get out of this bar, Im not in the mood to hear another drunkards tale."

Olavo then, already dizzy from the cachaça, leaned against the counter and said:
"Bah, not even one more sip of pinga, Garrafeiro?"

Jurandir snorted while cleaning one of the cups with an old rag:
"Pay your tab, Dias, and head back before night falls and trouble comes for you or your dear 'Laura'."

He then thought to himself:
"Disgusting men who think theyre 'men' only because of this but their places are already marked in hell the air here is so heavy it feels solid..."

. .

While the tension lingered in the bar, in Olavos simple wooden hut, "Laura" was visited by a slender, dark-skinned man with black hair down to his shoulders with a few strands stuck to his forehead as if he had been sweating from running, his skin marked by simple scars and ochre body paint and covered only by a simple leather loincloth and a necklace of seeds.

He stretched his hand toward the huts window, where "Laura" was. He then looked directly into her brown eyes, which seemed fearfulbut not of the man, of something else.

"Tayrikua..." He said, his voice breathless. That was "Lauras" true name. The man she knew, he was her younger brother, only 17 years old. She placed her hand on the window against his and spoke:
"Ñanguarú..."

She then opened the window and stepped out beside her brother, her linen apron snagging on a nail and tearing a bit, but she didnt care, she only wanted to flee that place she had been trapped for a year. They embraced, her brothers calloused body contrasting with her linen clothing, a gesture of affection. Ñanguarú then brushed his hand against his sisters face and murmured to himself:
"What did they do to you, sister..."

But then quickly looked around to check if any of the pale men were nearby, and then said:
"Lets leave here before they arrive, ok?"

She nodded, grabbing her brothers hand, and both fled into the prairies, heading wherever he was going. Ñanguarú guided her, holding tightly while scanning the surroundings. Each stumble was a held breath, until they reached a small hill to rest briefly. It was safefor at that hour in the late afternoon, the settlers were too drunk to go "hunting."

Tayrikua sighed and said:
"Where are we going, brother?"

He smiled, somewhat tired, his white teeth shining, and replied:
"To a safe place, sister to a better place..."

After a few minutes of rest, they resumed walking through the prairies and tall grass until they reached another rise...

At the top of the hill was their new home. The village was built on a hill surrounded by pointed wooden stakes, the longhouses were low but long, since Kanupé families were notably large. In the center of the village, a great fire burned and a map lay beside it, made of woven leaves with red pigments for danger, blue for water, and black for trails. One of the village elders, an old man wearing a feathered cloak, approached the young woman, looked her over briefly, then smiled and placed a hand on her shoulder:

Far from Encruzilhada and Olavos tension, further south lived Celestino Gonçalves, who had managed to make his lands productive with cattle raising and the cultivation of beans and corn. Three young Kaingangs, walking unclothed, stared at him. They were unarmed, but the tension was undeniable. The Bravanese settler felt his heart pounding against his chest in worry. But, unlike what he expected, the natives seemed to want to offer something. When he approached cautiously, they left a gift and then fled.

Celestino approached the giftit seemed to be a piece of smoked venison on a wooden plate wrapped in an araucaria leaf, which bore in barely legible scribbled letters the word "peace."

Surprised by the gift, Celestino picked it up gratefully, then gave a light nudge to his horse, just to make it rise, saying:
"Get up, Pé de Pano."

The horse obeyed, and Celestino mounted, preparing to return to his cabin, where his wife Maria awaited him.

Her hands were calloused from work, yet her serene and calm expression set her apart from other women who already seemed much older than their years. Maria was well cared for in her appearance overall. Surprised by the ready-made meat, she asked her husband:
"Where did you get this meat Tino?"

Thats what she called her husband, although she already knew the answer, she asked anyway. He replied:
"From neighbors who decided to help me with my hunt, Mari, just look at this."

She gave a subtle smile, already knowing who the "neighbors" he spoke of were.

The next day, at Celestinos request, Maria left an offering for the natives who had helped himan old hoe they no longer used and which was only taking up space. By sunset, the hoe was gone, and barefoot tracks led into the tall grass.

Article 4 stated that settlers could shoot the "savages" at will, but not all followed it strictly. Men like Celestino are a perfect example, a harmony that fools like Olavo could never understand...
[b] Story of Benício Moreira - 1809 [/b]

The avenger of the Pampas, a man who enforced the law by himself, Benício Moreira lived from 1769 until his death in the Revolt of the White Handkerchiefs in 1824.

The avenger of the Pampas was a man with a robust body and little hair, wore a straw-style sombrero and a white scarf around his neck. On his belt, in addition to a rifle, he carried a machete and muleteer boots, a leather vest, and finally two bandoliers crossed over his chest. He smoked a thick cigar and then threw it to the ground. He picked up a wanted poster:

[b] ULISSES HORSETAIL [/b]
WANTED DEAD OR ALIVE.
REWARD: 15 thousand Réis.

"Fifteen thousand Réis for this kid?"

Benício frowned, doubtful if the man on the poster was really worth that much. He was a boy of at least 20 years old; the drawing on the poster showed him with a broad nose, dark eyes, and a large ponytail that reached his back.

He looked at the back of the poster to analyze the reason for the above-average reward (5 thousand Réis for the region). It read:
"Hm stole horses and cattle, provisions, and smuggled dried meat and cachaça modest, seems a bit exaggerated even..."

He commented, straightening the crumpled paper in his pocket.
"Just over 20 and this kid already has a decent reward, huh"

He gave a smile and licked his lips:
"I will hunt any cangaceiro to hell as I have promised myself against any of these scoundrels"

The avenger then left and followed track after track until reaching Encruzilhada. He knew that "Garrafeiro" could also be an excellent informant, since he had dealt with various other taverns. The aura the avenger carried was strong and emanated; the other drinkers stepped back when Benício slammed the poster against the counter. Garrafeiro looked and said:
"Always straight to the point, Benício good morning."

The avenger greeted back with a gesture and then pointed to the poster:
"Jurandir you are the eyes and ears of these pampas, you must certainly know about this young cangaceiro."

Jurandir hesitated for a moment, wiped the glass in his hand for a few moments before finally responding:
"Look Ulisses, a cocky kid whos been beaten more than his father, now staying at the Esteira Ranch thinking the world owes him but look, I sell cachaça and drinks to drunks, not information to"

Benício smiled, already having what he wanted, took out some money, about a thousand Réis, placed it on the counter, and left. Jurandirs eyes gleamed at the money; he then whispered:
"but for a price I accept, Benício!"

He shouted to the avenger, who stopped to listen:
"Just know hes not alone, Horse Tail created his own gang, the Horse Tails, said to be about nine"

Moraes just smiled, rolling the machete between his fingers, and said:
"9 heads plus the leader himself, 10"

He then left the tavern, mounting his black horse, heading into the Pampas toward the last place Ulisses was seen. He didnt need to push, the animal galloped quickly under Benícios guidance, until he finally noticed smoke. It could be anything: a camp, a village, but it wasnt a hilly or river region, nor with many animalsit seemed intentionally isolated. Thats what Benício went to check. Leaving his horse, he leaned against a rock and observed: 9 men, and one more inside a tent. That was the refuge of the Horse Tail gang, its members raising a flag with a rearing horse, their members notable for having ponytails, obviously, and the largest was Ulisses, easy to recognize.

Benício began to observe. He wouldnt attack directlyhe wasnt a hero from stories, of courseso he waited patiently until late afternoon, when a nervous-looking youth was assigned to the watch. The avenger seized the opportunity and stealthily approached from behind, placing the machete against the boys throat and said:
"I dont intend to kill you, kid, tell me where your boss is."

Nervous and scared, the watchman pointed to one of the tents. The avenger then knocked him out with a strike to the neck, picked up a stone, and threw it elsewhere to draw the gang members attention.

The avenger went toward the tent the boy had indicated, where he found Ulisses adjusting a revolver. Hearing the intruder, he turned to shoot, but Benício was faster, throwing his machete that pierced his hand and forced him to drop the revolver. Horse Tail shouted, alerting the rest of the gang. Benício snorted:
"Damn"

The avenger ripped the blade from Horse Tails hand and then went toward the campfire. With his boots, he kicked embers into one of the tents that had gunpowder, exploding some of the men. The few inside panicked trying to save the camps provisions. Taking advantage of the chaos, the avenger tied up and slung Ulisses over his shoulder and ran to his horse, mocking:
"Seems your men care more about their own treasure than you."

[b]TCHOOSSS[/b].

The sound of a rifle shot echoed; the cocked weapon fired at Benício. For a fraction of a second, he froze, then dodged, the bullet grazing his face. He turned, grabbed a revolver, and fired at the shooter, not knowing if he hit, then ran again, listening to Horse Tails ramblings:
"Hein, want money? I can give you whatever you want, just untie me!"
"SHUT UP."

He roared, striking the cangaceiros with the revolver, rendering him unconscious, then mounted his horse and headed to Encruzilhada, hoping to earn about 15 thousand Réis and buy some cigars and new weapons. And thats how, riding into the horizon, he took down the "Horse Tail."
[b] São Damião de Figueiroa [/b]

Thats what Damião de Figueiroas followers called him. He was the one who rebelled against the coronels and led the Revolt of the White Handkerchiefs. He was nothing more than a pastor of a small chapel, but with undeniable charisma, and he created the first jagunços, the ex-cangaceiros hired as mercenaries

Damião was not a hero, nor anything special. He was born in a poor ranch and was a simple pastor of a small chapel in Boa Vista, carrying not the same Bible as the altars of São José, only a book of psalms and verses with his own interpretation of them.

He was of average height, without striking features, just a pastor like any other. However, in 1817, with the end of the First Contestado War, the arrival of the coronels with documents from São José approved by the emperor, and the lack of limitations, the coronels essentially took lands from smaller colonists who had spent the last 10 years fighting against the indigenous and conquering the region. His chapel soon ceased to be a mere center of solace, becoming a home for the homeless. The city ceased to be Boa Vista; the people would call it Hope.

In that humble chapel, they found comfort and a voice. The pastor did not preach violence but demanded divine justice. According to him, the coronels were not oppression, but a divine test, and as such, to be overcome.

At first, the coronels did not care. After all, to them he was just a simple pastor preaching. But the movement began to gain power and a name: [b]The White Handkerchiefs[/b], because the movement used white handkerchiefs to differentiate themselves. It was founded.

"bring down the coronels, and the holy land will be conquered."

Thats what he said. According to him, the holy land was the west itself, which had been conquered and now must be reconquered.

The revolt began in 1820. After a peaceful procession across the pampas, one of the coronels opened fire on the faithful, and that sparked a protest against oppression. Many responded: miserable peasants, muleteers, and even absolved cangaceiros called Jagunços. Even legends like the then-retired Justiceiro dos Pampas, Benício Moraes, joined the revolt. The holy army, as they called themselves, moved.

They moved like agile guerrillas. The coronels lands were invaded, they were killed, their families expelled, and the lands returned to their former owners. The jagunços were even more brutal, invading the big houses and executing the coronel and his family as a whole. The prophet São Damião was often seen wearing his white handkerchief around his neck, a faded colorful blanket, while wearing simple clothes underneath and muleteer boots, always carrying an old wooden staff adorned with rosaries and rice seed necklaces.

His appearance was nothing different from an ordinary man, sun-weathered skin, looking about 40 years old, but he always walked with confidence and absolute calm. He wandered the fields while healing the wounded in a way described as [b]magical[/b], as if the very skin of the injured healed in his mere presence.

An exceptional case of his miracles was saving a boy named Teodoro, who had suffered a destructive machete cut that almost killed him. Damião seemed to weave his skin with a gesture and then healed him, as if the wound had never existed.

[b] Organization of the White Handkerchiefs [/b]

The Messiah was the leader, Damião Figueiroa, or São Damião.

Below him were the 4 Sacred Knights:
[b]Master of Arms[/b] Benício Moraes.
[b]Master of Horses[/b] Bento Serrano.
[b]Master of Altars[/b] Celestino Gonçalves.
[b]Guardian of Faith[/b] Lourenço Costa.

Below them were the Devoted Blades, all women. They had no special titles, called South Wind, North Wind, East Wind, and West Wind.

[b]South Wind:[/b] Maria Gonçalves (Celestinos space)
[b]North Wind:[/b] Josefina dos Santos
[b]West Wind:[/b] Gertrudes Costa
[b]East Wind:[/b] Francisca Vieira

[b]Eyes of the Pampas[/b] was the title given to Jurandir Garrafeiro, an informant serving both sides, only taking what paid more.

The army was composed of a mix of militiamenmen, women, and elderscalled Divine Lancers. The tropeiros were the ones on horseback, making up most of the force and moving quickly.
[b]Esperança, 1824.[/b]

The Messiah picked up a guitar, his followers gathered around a bonfire, and he began to play along with a harmonica by his side.

"Your pilcha marked by bullets,
proved loyalty
You freed the frets in the rusgent wind,
drawing the dagger with cries of freedom"

The crowd sang along with the song, full of excitement and energy, while the fire crackled under the moonlight. Benício, the Justiceiro dos Pampas, sharpened his peixeira while leaning against a rock, observing Damião. He was not blindly faithful like many of the believers, he simply saw him as true justice. On the other side, Celestino and Maria were also presentnot mere colonists anymore, now high-ranking officers in the army of the Faithful.

After the music ended, Damião stood tall with his staff and began a speech.

"Brothers and sisters!"

He raised his voice:

"The cowardly coronel Valente will be our target tomorrow morning. As soon as the sun rises, we will advance to the Chapadão farm and destroy one of the dens of this evil that corrodes the holy land!"

The faithful rose in response, white-handkerchief flags waving, clearly exciteda fervor whose heat rivaled that of the bonfire.

The march began at dawn. Muleteers armed with sickles and spears, infantry with rifles, all ready for the invasion. Right behind were the Justiceiro dos Pampas and Master of Horses Bento Serrano. Years of war had turned the farm from a rural property into what Damião called a fortress: tall palisades dominated, and wire nets above prevented entry. Thats when the justiceiro suggested:

"Bento, I need you to launch a charge at the main gate. Ill find a way to open a path through the west."

Serrano hesitated at firstit was risky, he knew, and Benício was no longer youngbut there was no choice but to trust the plan.

Hidden, small but wide enough for a man to pass, the entry point was a fetid darkness Benício had to traverse. But justice would prevail. Emerging through one of the pig pens, he nearly vomited but resisted, listening to the warriors noise at the gate. Shots rang out as he dashed, firing his rifle from behind the farm guards, then slashing with his knife, tearing through flesh. Confusion spread among the guards.

The gate was opened, and chaos erupted. Thats when the justiceiro saw [i]him.[/i]

Valente was a large, robust man, aiming his rifle not at the chaos but at Bento, who led one of the charges.

"NO!"

Benício shouted, throwing himself against his comrade. The shot echoed across the battlefield, grazing his belt, ripping leather, burning his vest and shirt. He fell to the ground. The Master of Horses looked concerned, but Benício laughed:

"Youll have to try harder than that to take me down."

He stood, feeling tension in his shoulders, moving away from his ally, boots sinking in the muddy ground toward Valente on the veranda, then entered the main house. Valente aimed at him and smiled, firing again, but Benício ran, breaking through the door. The shot only shattered the window. Valente lunged at him, causing the justiceiro to drop his peixeira. Benício overpowered him, grabbing him with wide hands and throwing him against a wooden table, breaking it. Valente stamped on Benício with a sinister grin:

"Die, you filthy dog!"

Desperate, Benício groped for something to defend himself, the air thinning, pressure building on his neck. He grabbed a splintered piece of the broken table and drove it into Valente, forcing him to release his grip. Benício took a moment to breathe, struggling to rise, heart hammering. Valente, limping, advanced again, grabbing Benícios neck, but he used the mans weak leg to his advantage, kicking hard, weakening the hold. He spun his body, making the large man crash through the window. Benício seized the moment, lunging with his peixeira, stabbing the robust man.

In a disgusting babble of curses and blood, Valente struck once more, using a slaughter knife that cut Benícios side, leaving a dark red mark. He staggered, and after killing the coronel, reached the gate where victory was already celebrated. A white-handkerchief flag was raised atop the farm. He fell to his knees; the celebration turned from hostility to despair. One of the horsemen was fatally wounded, and the only one who could save him was Damião. The Messiah bent toward Benício, ready to act, but he gripped Damiãos arm:

"Ndont save me, dont hold me, Damião Ive done my part now let justice do the rest"

The voice gurgled through blood. He looked at the faithful warriors, smiled, and finally closed his eyes for eternal rest. His black horse neighed softly, then lay down beside his fallen friend.

[b]Serro dos Anjos, 1827.[/b]

Seven years of war, tens of thousands of deaths, but an effect that reverberated across the nation. Since the imperial army moved in, the revolt had become a series of guerrilla operations, now reduced to no more than 1,000 militiamen. Most of the Devoted Blades and all Knights were exterminated, leaving only Maria and Francisca. Damião climbed a high rock, using it as an altar, and declared:

"Brothers and sisters."

As he spoke and raised his staff, a mist enveloped them, obscuring the vision of the imperials. The Baron of Caçapava cursed:

"Damn it seems even the heavens want to protect this madman! ADVANCE TO THE HILL!"

He ordered, pointing his saber at the rebels.

"The empire does not know that faith cannot be killed, but spreads. They think they have cornered us, surrounded us, but they are [b]wrong[/b]."

He pointed his staff at everyone in front of him.

"Each one here is already victorious, each one already a guardian of these pampas. For hope, FOR THE HOLY LAND, DEFEND THIS SACRED HILL!"

The sound of advancing soldiers began. Soldiers with bayonets fired mercilessly as rebels were massacred, blood staining their white handkerchiefs. Francisca asked:

"Holiness, what do we do now?"

Damião smiled:

"Focus on the now, my dear sister."

He stepped in front of her, staff taking shots behind him yet remaining unscathed. He declared:

"Aarons Staff is unbreakable. Surrender and accept the divine light!"

He raised the staff again, reflecting the sun into a blinding beam, stunning the imperials and giving a brief advantage. But the imperials were poised to win. One by one, they fell

Maria fell among the bodies to avoid death. Francisca took a fatal shot to the heart. Only Damião remained standing. The Baron of Caçapava, curious, finally approached the rebel leader:

"Surrender, madman. Your madness has ruled these pampas far longer than it should"

Damião raised his arms, stepping backnot in fear, but as if declaiming:

"Who is victorious here? I fought for Gods will and an altar, you for a distant emperor and a hill. I for the people and the end of the coronels who among us truly wins?"

He spoke calmly, a terrifying peace in his tone. Then, in a surprising gesture, he raised his staff and said:

"The Holy Land is not conquered with blood, but sanctified with it!"

With surprising force, the White Handkerchief pierces the staff into the ground, even breaking the altar he stood on, then fell. A thunderous sound and tremor toppled many soldiers. Those who remained forced themselves to kneel. The Baron, shocked, exclaimed:

"Earthquake? Even the earth sides with this madman?!"

As he fell, Damiãos Bible dropped with him. One verse was marked inside:
[i]"He whose voice [b]then shook the Earth[/b]."[/i]

Maria, having seen everything, gripped the white handkerchief around her neck, also shocked, murmuring:

"So thats what the prophet meant?"

On the other side, horses neighed and soldiers kneeled as dust rose, sabers embedded in the ground, rifles fallen before them

This wild period would end with the arrival of Empress Isabel to the throne and the construction of new railways, the abolition of the Free Possession Law in 1890, and in general greater control of this frontier by the mid-1900s.
This period reached its peak three times: the first between 18101817, which ended with the First Contestado War (caused by settlers dissatisfaction with the lack of defined lands and property. In the end, the imperial government granted many lands to colonels, hoping they would maintain order in the region, but this lasted only until 1820 with the War of the White Scarves, when under Damião de Figueiroa the former settlers revolted with the promise of receiving a "holy land." The war lasted seven years and caused 20,000 deaths. In the end, the colonels were removed from their lands and the empire opted to let settlers return to having their properties. This caused the second peak, which was significantly longer, from 1830 to 1865, a total of 35 years, amidst robberies, conflicts with natives, the land was seen as lawless but rich with opportunity.
In 1865 until 1872, there was the Revolt of the White Scarves, which was a revolt against the construction of railways in the region that displaced many settlers and left them with nothing, and many towns ended up abandoned. This war was, according to the rebels, against the company and not the empire. Here, cangaceiros, monks, cangaceiros, and peasants united in war, very different sides coming together against the army, numbering over 100,000 rebels. Of the three Contestado Wars, this was undoubtedly the most brutal and ended with 60,000 dead on both sides, most of them rebels. This event caused the slow decline of the Wild Pampas until 1890.

[b] Kanupés and Olavo [/b] A compilation of stories about the conquest of the region. He gave her a farewell kiss and left on horseback toward Encruzilhada, a small settlement located at a three-way crossroads.

The simple place, whose center was a tavern in the warehouse with a stained wooden counter and barrels of liquor and drunkards collapsed on the floor.

A dispute then began, each of the drunken men there started telling increasingly exaggerated stories of victories against natives, each one more far-fetched than the last.

Olavo then, already dizzy from the cachaça, leaned against the counter and said:

Jurandir snorted while cleaning one of the cups with an old rag:

. .

While the tension lingered in the bar, in Olavos simple wooden hut, "Laura" was visited by a slender, dark-skinned man with black hair down to his shoulders with a few strands stuck to his forehead as if he had been sweating from running, his skin marked by simple scars and ochre body paint and covered only by a simple leather loincloth and a necklace of seeds.

"What did they do to you, sister..."

"Lets leave here before they arrive, ok?"

Tayrikua sighed and said:
"Where are we going, brother?"

"To a safe place, sister to a better place..."

After a few minutes of rest, they resumed walking through the prairies and tall grass until they reached another rise...

One of the village elders, an old man wearing a feathered cloak, approached the young woman, looked her over briefly, then smiled and placed a hand on her shoulder:

[b] Story of Celestino - 1808. [/b]

Far from Encruzilhada and Olavos tension, further south lived Celestino Gonçalves, who had managed to make his lands productive with cattle raising and the cultivation of beans and corn. Celestino approached the giftit seemed to be a piece of smoked venison on a wooden plate wrapped in an araucaria leaf, which bore in barely legible scribbled letters the word "peace."

Surprised by the gift, Celestino picked it up gratefully, then gave a light nudge to his horse, just to make it rise, saying:
